lesson.lesson_summary: Learn how English words belong to two main groups: open classes, which can easily gain new words, and closed classes, which usually have a fixed set of words. Discover their differences, identify their members and understand how they work in everyday sentences.

learning_dimensions.dimension: Common Learner Mistakes and Error Correction

pages.title: Two Groups of Words

content.text: English has thousands of words. But words do not all behave in the same way. We can divide them into two big groups: open word classes and closed word classes.

examples.explanation: These words belong to open word classes. Other words belong to closed word classes.

pages.key_takeaway: English words belong to two main groups.

pages.title: What Is an Open Class?

content.text: An open word class is a group that can easily welcome new words. English speakers create and borrow words to talk about new things.

examples.explanation: Google began as a name. It is now also used as a verb.
Selfie is a relatively modern word added to English vocabulary.

pages.key_takeaway: Open classes can easily gain new words.

pages.title: What Is a Closed Class?

content.text: A closed word class is a group with a relatively fixed set of words. New words are rarely added because these words mainly help us build sentences.

examples.sentence: She is sitting on the chair.
examples.explanation: These words belong to closed word classes. They help connect and organise the sentence.

content.title: Remember
content.text: Closed does not mean that no new word can ever enter the group. It means that new additions are uncommon.

pages.key_takeaway: Closed classes usually have a fixed set of words.

pages.title: The Four Open Classes

content.text: There are four main open word classes. They carry much of the meaning in our sentences.

items: Nouns – name people, places, things or ideas.
Lexical verbs – express actions, events or states.
Adverbs – modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or whole clauses.

examples.explanation: Child is a noun, plays is a verb, happy is an adjective and happily is an adverb.

pages.key_takeaway: Nouns, lexical verbs, adjectives and adverbs are the main open classes.

pages.title: The Closed Word Classes

content.text: Closed word classes contain words that help sentences work. They show relationships, point to people or things, and connect ideas.

items: Pronouns – I, you, he, she, they.
Determiners – a, an, the, this, some.
Prepositions – in, on, under, at, with.
Auxiliary verbs – be, have and do when used as helping verbs, and modal auxiliaries such as can and must.
Particles – words such as not and the infinitive marker to, in their grammatical uses.

pages.key_takeaway: Closed classes help words work together in sentences.

pages.title: Open Versus Closed

items.label: Closed classes
items.description: Usually have a relatively fixed set of words.

comparison_points: Open classes mainly carry lexical meaning.
Closed classes mainly provide grammatical structure.
New vocabulary is added more easily to open classes.
content.conclusion: Both groups are important for making meaningful sentences.

pages.key_takeaway: Open classes grow more easily than closed classes.

pages.title: See Both Groups Together

examples.sentence: The clever boy ran into the garden.
examples.explanation: Clever is an adjective, boy is a noun and ran is a verb. The and into are closed-class words: a determiner and a preposition.
She is a pronoun, sings is a verb and beautifully is an adverb.

pages.key_takeaway: One sentence can contain words from both groups.

pages.title: How to Identify Them

content.text: Look at what a word does in a sentence. Does it name, describe or express an action? It may belong to an open class. Does it connect, point or show a relationship? It may belong to a closed class.

examples.sentence: A cat slept under the table.
examples.explanation: Cat and table are nouns, slept is a verb, while a and the are determiners and under is a preposition.

pages.key_takeaway: Identify a word by its job in the sentence.

pages.title: Check What You Know

content.text: Let's practise identifying open and closed word classes. Read each question carefully and think about the job of the word.

pages.key_takeaway: Look at the word's grammatical job.

pages.title: Why Are They Open?

content.text: People invent new things and new ways to communicate. English needs new words to describe them. New nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs can enter the language.

examples.explanation: App is a modern noun. Download is also used as a verb.

pages.key_takeaway: New ideas bring new open-class vocabulary.

pages.title: Why Are They Closed?

content.text: Words such as the, and, in and she perform basic grammatical jobs. English usually does not need new words for these jobs, so their groups change very slowly.

examples.sentence: She put the book on the table.
examples.explanation: These established grammatical words show who, which thing and where.

content.title: Remember
content.text: Closed classes are not completely frozen. Their membership can change over time, but additions are uncommon.

pages.key_takeaway: Closed classes change slowly because their grammatical jobs are established.

pages.title: One Word, Two Jobs

content.text: Some words can belong to different word classes in different sentences. Their grammatical job depends on how they are used.

content.conclusion: Always examine the word in its sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: A word's class depends on how it is used.

pages.title: Some Special Cases

content.text: Not every word fits perfectly into a simple open-or-closed list. Some grammar books classify certain words differently. Interjections, such as wow and oh, are often treated separately.

examples.explanation: Wow is an interjection. It expresses a sudden feeling. Its classification may vary across grammatical frameworks.

content.title: Important
content.text: This lesson focuses on the main open and closed word classes. Some advanced grammar systems use more detailed classifications.

pages.key_takeaway: Some words need a closer look before classification.

pages.title: Avoid This Mistake

content.text: Do not decide whether a word is open or closed just by looking at its spelling or meaning. First identify its grammatical job in the sentence.

mistake.correct: Text can be a noun or a verb.
mistake.reason: In 'I received a text', it is a noun. In 'I will text you', it is a verb. Both noun and lexical verb are open classes.

pages.key_takeaway: Classify words by their use, not just their form.

pages.title: Your Quick Revision

items: Open classes can easily gain new words.
The four main open classes are nouns, lexical verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
Closed classes usually contain a relatively fixed set of words.
Pronouns, determiners, prepositions and conjunctions are closed classes.
Auxiliaries and particles are also generally classified as closed classes.
A word's grammatical class depends on its job in a sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: Open classes grow. Closed classes provide grammatical structure.

question_bank.prompt: What is an open word class?

options.text: A group that can easily gain new words.
A group that contains only one word.

question_bank.explanation: An open word class can easily gain new words as the language develops.

question_bank.prompt: Closed word classes usually have a relatively fixed set of words.
question_bank.explanation: Correct. Closed classes usually gain new words very rarely.

question_bank.prompt: In the sentence 'The dog sleeps under the table', which word belongs to a closed class?
question_bank.explanation: Under is a preposition. Prepositions belong to closed word classes.

question_bank.prompt: Which group contains only open word classes?
question_bank.explanation: Nouns, lexical verbs, adjectives and adverbs are the four main open word classes.

question_bank.prompt: Match each word class with its correct group.
question_bank.explanation: Nouns and adjectives are open classes. Pronouns and prepositions are closed classes.

question_bank.prompt: In 'She sings beautifully', which word is a closed-class word?
question_bank.explanation: She is a pronoun, which belongs to a closed word class.

question_bank.prompt: New words can easily enter open word classes.
question_bank.explanation: Open classes welcome new vocabulary as people create new words and adopt words from other languages.

question_bank.prompt: Why do closed word classes usually change slowly?

options.text: They mainly perform established grammatical jobs.
They are not used in sentences.

question_bank.explanation: Closed-class words perform established grammatical jobs, so new additions are uncommon.

question_bank.prompt: In which sentence is 'text' used as a verb?
question_bank.explanation: In 'I will text you', text describes the action of sending a message, so it is a verb.

question_bank.prompt: Which statement correctly describes open and closed word classes?

options.text: Open classes can easily gain words, while closed classes usually change slowly.
Open classes contain only short words.
Closed classes contain all nouns and verbs.
Every word always belongs to the same class.

question_bank.explanation: Open classes grow more easily, while closed classes usually have relatively fixed membership.

question_bank.prompt: Which of these is a closed word class?
question_bank.explanation: Conjunctions such as and, but and because belong to closed word classes.

question_bank.prompt: In 'The little girl smiled happily', which word is an adjective?
question_bank.explanation: Little describes the noun girl, so it is an adjective and belongs to an open word class.

question_bank.prompt: A word always belongs to the same word class, whatever sentence it appears in.
question_bank.explanation: Some words can belong to different word classes depending on their grammatical use. Text, for example, can be a noun or a verb.
Those is a determiner when it comes before a noun, as in those books. Determiners belong to closed word classes.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the open-class word in this sentence: 'The children played outside.'
question_bank.explanation: Children is a noun. Nouns are open-class words.
